description: The Fellowship of One is a solo team driven by curiosity, science, and a love for building things. I'm fascinated by space, physics, and engineering, and enjoy turning ambitious ideas into working projects. This NASA Space Apps, I'm taking on the challenge of harmonising MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire observations to make fire activity easier to analyse and understand.
summary:
FireAtlas is a web-based tool that tackles the core problem of comparing fire detection data from two different satellite instruments: MODIS (1km resolution, running since 2000) and VIIRS (375m resolution, running since 2012). Because VIIRS detects roughly 4x more fires than MODIS for the same area, you can’t just merge their datasets and draw meaningful conclusions about long-term fire trends. FireAtlas solves this by computing a harmonization ratio from the 2012-2024 overlap period, when both instruments were active simultaneously. This ratio normalizes MODIS counts to the VIIRS scale, producing a continuous and consistent fire record from 2000 to 2024 across 195 countries.

The dashboard presents this through a calendar heatmap, a sensor timeline, confidence-level filtering, and a global heat grid with nearly 900,000 grid cells. Users can toggle between raw and harmonized views to see the difference the correction makes. The result is a practical tool that makes cross-sensor fire data actually comparable, which matters for studying long-term burning patterns and regional fire trends.
details:
What it does:

FireAtlas lets you explore 25 years of satellite fire detection data (2000-2024) through an interactive dashboard. Pick any of 195 countries, and you get a calendar heatmap showing daily burning activity, a timeline of which sensors were observing, stats on detection counts and seasonal peaks, and a global heat grid mapping fire density across nearly 900,000 grid cells worldwide.

The key feature is the harmonized view. MODIS and VIIRS are two different instruments with very different capabilities. MODIS has been running since 2000 on the Terra and Aqua satellites at 1km resolution. VIIRS joined in 2012 on Suomi NPP at 375m resolution, and because of that finer resolution, it picks up roughly 4x more fires in the same area. That makes it misleading to just stack their data together, because you’d see what looks like a massive spike in fires around 2012 that’s really just a sensor change.

How the harmonization works:

I computed the overall ratio of total VIIRS detections to total MODIS detections across the entire 2012-2024 overlap period (requiring a minimum of 6 months of overlapping data per country). This ratio captures how many more fires VIIRS sees compared to MODIS for a given region. In harmonized mode, the dashboard scales MODIS-era counts up by this ratio, so you get a continuous, apples-to-apples fire record stretching back to 2000. Users can toggle between raw and harmonized views to see exactly what the correction does.

Data pipeline:

I pulled all the data from NASA FIRMS using their API, covering both the MODIS_SP and VIIRS_SNPP_SP sources. That came out to over 415 million individual fire detections across 33GB of raw CSVs. I wrote Python scripts to process this into per-country JSON files containing daily detection counts broken down by instrument and confidence level, plus a summary file with harmonization ratios and country-level statistics. The heat grid was built by binning all detections into 0.1-degree grid cells with per-year breakdowns for total, MODIS, VIIRS, and high-confidence counts.

Tools and tech:

The whole thing is a static site: HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with no build step or framework. Leaflet handles the interactive map, Chart.js powers the calendar heatmap and charts, and GeoJSON boundaries from the geo-countries dataset provide the country outlines. I wrote the data processing pipeline in Python. The site is deployed on Vercel with the GitHub repo as the source.

What makes it creative:

Most fire data tools just show you dots on a map for a recent time window. FireAtlas goes back 25 years and directly addresses the sensor comparison problem that makes long-term fire analysis tricky. The calendar heatmap format makes seasonal patterns immediately visible, and the confidence filtering lets researchers focus on high-certainty detections. The harmonization toggle is something I haven’t seen in other fire visualization tools: it lets you see both the raw reality and the corrected view side by side, which is useful for understanding what the data actually means versus what the instruments happen to report.
